title: GitHub account and 2FA
plain: A GitHub account is your identity on github.com. Two-factor authentication (2FA) adds a second proof to your password, such as a code from an app on your phone.
check: If your phone broke tomorrow, how could you still sign in to GitHub, and where would you find what you need?
rubric: Opens Settings, then Password and authentication, and points to a 2FA method that is turned on.
Says where the recovery codes are stored (a password manager or paper) and that they are not in any repository or chat.
Finds Emails in Settings and says whether the address is verified and whether Keep my email addresses private is on.
try: Open github.com in your browser, click your profile picture, choose Settings, then Password and authentication. You should see at least one two-factor method marked as enabled and a Recovery codes entry with a View button. If you see an Enable two-factor authentication button instead, 2FA is not on yet: turn it on with an authenticator app. Check that your recovery codes are saved in a password manager or on paper. Never type a password or code into this chat.
pitfall: Wrong belief: if I lose my phone, GitHub Support can always restore my account. Correct: with 2FA on, GitHub Support cannot restore access if you lose both your 2FA method and your recovery methods, so save the recovery codes now.

title: GitHub repository
plain: A repository on GitHub is a project's files and their full history, stored online. The README.md file in it is shown on the repository's main page.
check: A stranger opens your repository page. What will the README tell them, and what would they still not know about your project?
rubric: Creates the repository on github.com with visibility set to Private and Add README turned on.
Opens the repository page and points to the text on it that comes from README.md.
Says what a stranger would learn from the README and what is still missing.
try: On github.com click the + icon in the upper-right corner, choose New repository, name it hello-practice, choose Private, turn on Add README and click Create repository. You should see a file list that contains README.md, with the README text shown below the files. Nothing from your computer is uploaded, and you can delete the repository later in its Settings.
pitfall: Wrong belief: creating a repository on GitHub puts my project folder on GitHub. Correct: it creates an online repository that is empty (or holds only files you chose, such as a README); your computer's folder is connected to it only after you add a remote and push.

title: Connect project to GitHub
signals: does not appear to be a git repository
plain: To connect your project to GitHub, create an empty repository there and add it as the remote origin. Then push your commits, so GitHub holds a copy of your saved history.
check: Your first git push is rejected, and the GitHub repository has a README that you created in the browser. Why was the push rejected, and what is the safe next step?
rubric: Says the push was rejected because the GitHub repository holds a commit (the README) that the computer's history does not contain.
Does not use git push --force; for a practice project, creates a new empty repository, or asks for help to combine the two histories.
Creates the GitHub repository as Private and empty, links it with git remote add origin <address> and reads git remote -v.
try: In a practice project that has at least one commit and a .gitignore, first run git ls-files (the files Git tracks) and check that no key or .env file is listed. On github.com create a Private repository with no README, license or .gitignore. Copy its HTTPS address, then run git remote add origin <that address>, git branch --show-current (it should print main; if it prints master, run git branch -M main) and git push -u origin main. If Git asks you to sign in, use the browser sign-in described in the GitHub authentication card. Reload the repository page: your files and commits appear. One-step alternative: gh repo create hello-practice --private --source=. --remote=origin --push.
pitfall: Wrong belief: for a project that already exists on my computer, I should create the GitHub repository with a README first. Correct: then GitHub has a commit that your computer lacks, and the first push is rejected. Create the GitHub repository empty, then push.

title: GitHub CLI (gh)
plain: The GitHub CLI, with the command gh, lets you use GitHub from the terminal. It can view repositories and open pull requests. It is a separate program from git and works only with GitHub.
check: You want to read your local commit history and also open a pull request. Which of the two jobs needs git, which needs gh, and how can you tell?
rubric: Runs gh --version and says what the output shows: the program is installed, and its version.
Runs gh repo view --json name,visibility,url in a folder linked to GitHub and reads the visibility value.
Says which commands belong to git (local history) and which to gh (GitHub features such as pull requests).
try: Run gh --version: it prints a line such as gh version 2.x.x. If the command is not found, install gh from cli.github.com and open a new terminal. In a folder linked to a GitHub repository, run gh repo view --json name,visibility,url. You should see JSON with the repository name, its address and a visibility of PRIVATE or PUBLIC. If gh says you are not logged in, continue with the GitHub authentication card.
pitfall: Wrong belief: gh and git are the same tool. Correct: git saves versions on your computer and works with any host; gh talks to GitHub's own features (pull requests, issues, releases) and needs you to be logged in.

title: GitHub authentication
plain: Authentication proves to GitHub who you are when your computer pushes or pulls. Use gh auth login, a personal access token, or an SSH key. Your account password no longer works for Git.
check: A helper in a chat says: paste your token here and I will fix your push. What do you do, and what do you do if you already sent it?
rubric: Completes gh auth login with the web browser option; the sign-in happens in the browser, not in the terminal.
Runs gh auth status and reads the account name, the Git protocol and where the token is kept (keyring means the system credential store).
Says that a token is never pasted into chat, code, a commit or a screenshot, and that gh auth status --show-token is not needed.
try: Run gh auth status. If it says you are logged in to github.com, read the account name and the word in brackets after it. If it says you are not logged in, run gh auth login, choose GitHub.com, choose HTTPS, answer Y when asked to authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials, then choose Login with a web browser and follow the steps. Never run gh auth status with --show-token.
pitfall: Wrong belief: any token will do, so I can create one with every permission to avoid errors. Correct: a classic personal access token with the repo scope reaches all your repositories. Prefer gh auth login or a fine-grained token limited to one repository, and revoke a leaked token at once.

title: Public or private repository
plain: A public repository can be read by anyone on the internet. A private repository can be read only by you and people you invite. Making a private repository public publishes its whole history.
check: You kept a repository private for a month and deleted a file with a password from it last week. You now want to make it public. What will strangers be able to see, and what do you do before you click the button?
rubric: States that every commit and every older version of every file becomes readable, not only the current files.
States that a key committed earlier and deleted later is still exposed and must be revoked.
Names two checks to do before the switch, such as a search of the history for secrets and a look for personal data in files.
try: Run gh repo view --json visibility,url in a folder linked to GitHub, or look for the Public or Private label next to the repository name on github.com. Then run git log --oneline and imagine every line readable by strangers. Write down anything in those commits that you would not want them to see. Do not change the visibility yet.
pitfall: Wrong belief: I can make a repository public and take it back later with no harm. Correct: once it is public anyone can fork or clone it, and making it private again does not remove those copies. Treat the switch to public as one-way.

title: Fork
plain: A fork is your own copy of someone else's repository, stored in your GitHub account. You can change your copy freely and ask the original owner to take your changes with a pull request.
check: You fork a project, edit README.md in your fork and commit. What changes in the original repository, and how could the original owner get your edit?
rubric: Says the change exists only in the fork; the original (upstream) repository does not change until a pull request is merged.
Says a fork does not update itself when the original changes, so it has to be synced.
Says a branch lives inside one repository while a fork is a separate repository.
try: On github.com open github.com/octocat/Spoon-Knife, GitHub's practice repository, click Fork and then Create fork. You land on a page for your own copy, with the line forked from octocat/Spoon-Knife under the title. When you are done, delete the practice fork in its Settings, in the Danger Zone section.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a fork is the same as a branch, or it stays up to date by itself. Correct: a branch lives inside one repository, a fork is a separate repository, and a fork has to be synced with the original (the Sync fork button, or git).

title: GitHub issues
plain: A GitHub issue is a numbered note about a bug, task or idea in a repository. People comment on it, label it and close it. The command gh issue works with issues in the terminal.
check: A pull request description says Closes #12, but issue 12 is still open after the pull request was merged. What could explain that?
rubric: Creates an issue with gh issue create or the New issue button and reads its number.
Lists it with gh issue list and closes it with gh issue close <number>.
Writes Closes #<number> in a pull request description and says the issue closes only when that pull request is merged into the default branch.
try: In a private practice repository run gh issue create --title "Button does nothing" --body "Click Save on the settings page: nothing happens. Expected: the settings are saved." It prints the address of the new issue, which ends with a number such as /issues/1. Run gh issue list to see it, then gh issue close 1. Without gh, use the Issues tab and the New issue button.
pitfall: Wrong belief: an issue is a private note to myself. Correct: in a public repository anyone can read issues and comments, so never paste keys, tokens, logs that contain secrets or personal data into one.

title: Pull request
plain: A pull request (PR) asks the owner of a repository to merge the changes from one branch into another branch. People can read the changes, comment on them and approve them before the merge.
check: Codex opened a pull request for you. Before you click Merge, which tabs of the page do you open, and what are you looking for in each?
rubric: Opens the pull request page and reads the title, the description and the checks on the Conversation tab.
Opens Files changed and names one added line (green) and one removed line (red).
Says what to look for before Merge: the files match the task, no secrets, and the checks pass.
try: In a private practice repository run git switch -c try/readme-line, add one line to README.md, then run git add README.md, git commit -m "Add a practice line" and git push -u origin try/readme-line. Run gh pr create --fill, or click Compare & pull request on github.com. You should see a page whose Files changed tab shows your one added line. Close it without merging: gh pr close <number>.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a pull request pulls code onto my computer, or merges by itself. Correct: it is a request on GitHub to merge one branch into another; nothing changes in the target branch until someone clicks Merge.

title: Reviewing a pull request
plain: Reviewing a pull request means reading its changed lines on the Files changed tab. You comment on lines, then choose Comment, Approve or Request changes. You cannot approve your own pull request.
check: A pull request for changing a button colour touches 14 files, including package.json and a file named .env. Which changes make you stop before approving, and what do you ask?
rubric: Opens Files changed and reads every changed file, marking each one as Viewed.
Checks four things: the files match the task, no secrets or personal data, no new dependency without a reason, and the checks pass.
Leaves at least one comment on a specific line.
try: Open a pull request in your own practice repository (see the pull request card) and click Files changed. Hover over one changed line, click the blue comment icon and write a question. Click Start a review, then Review changes, choose Comment and click Submit review. Your comment appears on that line. In the terminal, gh pr diff <number> shows the same changes. Practise only on your own repository, because a submitted review is visible to everyone who can see the pull request.
pitfall: Wrong belief: green checks and a tidy description mean a pull request is safe to approve. Correct: checks only test what the tests cover, so read the changed files for secrets, new dependencies and changes outside the task. Request changes also does not block a merge unless a rule requires reviews.

title: GitHub security alerts
plain: Secret scanning finds keys committed to a repository. Push protection blocks a push that contains one. Dependabot warns about dependencies with known security problems. Which of them apply depends on visibility and plan.
check: You push a key to a private repository on a free personal account and GitHub says nothing. Why was there no warning, and which tool would have reacted if the repository were public?
rubric: Says that for a public repository, push protection for users blocks the push and secret scanning checks the repository.
Says that a private repository on a free personal account has no secret scanning or repository push protection, according to GitHub's documentation.
Concludes that .gitignore, reading git diff --cached before committing and revoking leaked keys are the learner's own safety net.
try: Open your repository on github.com, click Settings and find Advanced Security in the sidebar (it sits under a heading such as Security and quality, and the names change from time to time). Read which of Dependabot alerts, secret scanning and push protection are shown, and whether each one is on, off or not available for your repository. Change nothing yet.
pitfall: Wrong belief: GitHub will always stop me from pushing a secret. Correct: push protection for individuals covers public repositories on github.com and only recognises known key formats. A private repository on a free personal account has no secret scanning, so your own checks are the safety net.

title: GitHub Pages
plain: GitHub Pages publishes a static website (HTML, CSS and JavaScript files) from a repository. On a free account it needs a public repository, and the site is visible to everyone on the internet.
check: You built a recipe site with a contact form that saves messages in a database. Which part can GitHub Pages host, and which part can it not?
rubric: Puts index.html at the top level of the publishing folder and picks the source in Settings, then Pages.
Opens the github.io address and sees the page.
Says that every file in a public repository is public too, so no keys or personal data belong there.
try:
In a new practice PUBLIC repository that contains only a file index.html with the line

Hello

, open Settings, then Pages. Choose Deploy from a branch, branch main, folder / (root), and click Save. Wait up to 10 minutes, then open https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/REPOSITORY-NAME/ and you should see Hello. To take the site down, use the menu next to the Your site is live at message under GitHub Pages and choose Unpublish site, or delete the practice repository.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a Pages site from a private repository is private, or Pages works for any repository on a free account. Correct: Pages sites are public on the internet even when the repository is private (where the plan allows Pages), and on GitHub Free the repository must be public.

title: GitHub Actions
plain: GitHub Actions runs automated jobs, such as tests, on GitHub's computers. A job starts when an event happens in your repository, for example a push. The jobs are described in YAML files in .github/workflows.
check: A workflow file contains the line on: pull_request. When does the workflow run, and where on GitHub do you see whether it passed?
rubric: Finds the on: section and names the event that starts the workflow.
Finds jobs, runs-on and steps, and says what one step does.
Says where results appear: the Actions tab, and the Checks tab of a pull request.
try: Run gh run list -R cli/cli -L 3. It reads one public project and prints its three latest workflow runs, one per line, with the result, the workflow name, the branch and the event that started the run, such as push, pull_request or schedule. Nothing is changed. If gh answers To get started with GitHub CLI, please run: gh auth login, log in first (see the GitHub authentication card). In your own project, ls .github/workflows lists your workflow files; an error such as no such path means you have none yet.
pitfall: Wrong belief: Actions is free and harmless on any repository. Correct: it is free for public repositories on standard runners, while private repositories get a monthly allowance by plan and extra use is billed to the owner. A workflow also runs code, so read workflow changes in pull requests like any code.
